  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S8" title="In The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">8 </span>Conclusion</span></a></li>

</div><div class="ltx_page_content">
<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">The Geometry of Noise: 
<br class="ltx_break">Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mojtaba Sahraee-Ardakan
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mauricio Delbracio
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Peyman Milanfar
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Google
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Autonomous (noise-agnostic) generative models, such as Equilibrium Matching and blind diffusion, challenge the standard paradigm by learning a single, time-invariant vector field that operates without explicit noise-level conditioning. While recent work suggests that high-dimensional concentration allows these models to implicitly estimate noise levels from corrupted observations, a fundamental paradox remains: what is the underlying landscape being optimized when the noise level is treated as a random variable, and how can a bounded, noise-agnostic network remain stable near the data manifold where gradients typically diverge?</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p">We resolve this paradox by formalizing Marginal Energy, <math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log p(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log p(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="abstract1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt</annotation></semantics></math> is the marginal density of the noisy data integrated over a prior distribution of unknown noise levels. We prove that generation using autonomous models is not merely blind denoising, but a specific form of Riemannian gradient flow on this Marginal Energy. Through a novel relative energy decomposition, we demonstrate that while the raw Marginal Energy landscape possesses a <math id="abstract1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/t^{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/t^{p}</annotation></semantics></math> singularity normal to the data manifold, the learned time-invariant field implicitly incorporates a local conformal metric that perfectly counteracts the geometric singularity, converting an infinitely deep potential well into a stable attractor.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p">We also establish the structural stability conditions for sampling with autonomous models. We identify a “Jensen Gap” in noise-prediction parameterizations that acts as a high-gain amplifier for estimation errors, explaining the catastrophic failure observed in deterministic blind models. Conversely, we prove that velocity-based parameterizations are inherently stable because they satisfy a bounded-gain condition that absorbs posterior uncertainty into a smooth geometric drift.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h3>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative modeling has seen immense progress over the past decade, tracing its roots to the foundational non-equilibrium thermodynamics approach introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>. This paradigm was popularized and scaled by Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and subsequent architectural refinements <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, Score-based models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, and subsequently unified under the continuous-time mathematical framework of score-based stochastic differential equations (SDEs)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>. For a broader conceptual overview of how these perspectives on diffusion have evolved, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. More recently, the field has evolved beyond pure diffusion to embrace velocity-based transport formulations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, notably Flow Matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, as well as stationary targets like Equilibrium Matching (EqM)<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A defining characteristic of these standard generative models is their reliance on explicit time-conditioning. They typically learn a conditional score function or velocity field, such as <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math>, defining a dynamic field that changes with time, i.e. a field over <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{D}\times[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{D}\times[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>. In these frameworks, the network relies on the time variable <math id="S1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to dictate the current scale of corruption and orient the trajectory.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, recent work has explored autonomous approaches, such as EqM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> or noise-blind diffusion <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, which learn a single noise-agnostic vector field <math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\theta}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\theta}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> independent of <math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote the optimal vector field learned by such a model as <math id="S1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>. It is important to distinguish the model’s architecture from the resulting inference dynamics: while the sampling process may still utilize a time-dependent schedule to scale the trajectory, the underlying neural network is strictly time-invariant. This autonomous approach presents a fundamental puzzle: the “correct” gradient to follow from a point <math id="S1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> should depend heavily on its noise level. How can a single, static vector field effectively guide a sample from pure noise (high <math id="S1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>) and also guide a sample from light noise (low <math id="S1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>), all while ensuring its stationary points accurately reflect the clean data <math id="S1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we resolve this paradox. We show that such an autonomous model is not merely acting as a “blind” denoiser, but is implicitly learning a hybrid field that is fundamentally tied to a single, non-parametric marginal energy landscape (<math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math>). This energy is defined as the negative log-likelihood of the marginal data distribution <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S1.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S1.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log\left(\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt\right)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0em">∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log\left(\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We build our argument as follows:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Energy Paradox:</span> We define the marginal energy and derive its explicit gradient. We rigorously show that this gradient diverges near the data manifold, creating an infinitely deep potential well that forbids stable gradient descent.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Energy-Aligned Decomposition:</span> We analyze the learned autonomous vector fields, proving they decompose into exactly three geometric components: a natural gradient, a transport correction (covariance) term, and a linear drift.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Riemannian Gradient Flow:</span> We resolve the singularity paradox by showing that noise-agnostic models implicitly implement a Riemannian gradient flow. The learned vector field incorporates a local conformal metric (the effective gain) that perfectly preconditions and counteracts the geometric singularity of the raw energy landscape.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stability of Sampling with Autonomous Models:</span> We establish the mathematical conditions necessary for sampling stability. We prove that velocity-based parameterizations (e.g., Flow Matching, EqM) succeed because they absorb posterior uncertainty into a stable drift, whereas standard noise-prediction parameterizations (e.g., DDPM/DDIM) act as high-gain amplifiers for estimation errors, leading to structural instability.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our work unifies and grounds three recent lines of inquiry in generative modeling: noise unconditional generation, equilibrium dynamics, and energy-based training.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Noise-Blind Denoising.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The prevailing paradigm in score-based modeling relies on conditioning the network on the noise level <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. However, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. [30]</a></cite> recently challenged this, demonstrating that “blind” models can achieve high-fidelity generation without <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. This connects to earlier findings in image restoration by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gnanasambandam and Chan [11]</a></cite>, who showed that a single “one-size-fits-all” denoiser could approximate an ensemble of noise-specific estimators. Our work provides the rigorous theoretical justification for these observations, identifying <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math> as the implicit objective and connecting the gradients of this energy to the autonomous fields via concentration of the noise level given the noisy signal.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In concurrent work, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kadkhodaie et al. [15]</a></cite> provide a highly rigorous statistical analysis of blind denoising diffusion models (BDDMs) for data with low intrinsic dimensionality. They analytically prove that under the assumption that the intrinsic dimension is much smaller than the ambient dimension (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k\ll d</annotation></semantics></math>), BDDMs can accurately estimate the true noise level from a single observation and implicitly track a valid noise schedule, providing robust finite-time sampling guarantees. While their work offers an exhaustive and rigorous statistical treatment of this low-dimensional data regime, our work situates this concentration of measure as a specific asymptotic case (Regime I) within a broader geometric framework. Specifically, our focus lies in connecting noise-blind generation to the gradient of the marginal energy landscape, revealing the process as a Riemannian gradient flow. Furthermore, whereas their analysis focuses primarily on specific Langevin-type SDE discretizations, our framework is generalized across arbitrary affine diffusion processes and learning targets. Finally, while they demonstrate that blind denoisers can outperform non-blind counterparts by avoiding schedule mismatch errors, our framework allows us to prove why models trained to predict noise (e.g., DDPM/DDIM) are structurally unstable for autonomous generation due to gradient singularities, demonstrating why velocity- or signal-based targets are strictly necessary.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Energy Landscapes &amp; Singularities.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While the framework of energy-based learning is well-established <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, explicitly learning energy functions is known to be unstable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. Recent approaches like “Dual Score Matching” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> attempt to stabilize this by learning a joint energy via both space and time scores. Our work analyzes the <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginal</span> energy, aligning with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scarvelis et al. [25]</a></cite>, who proved that the exact closed-form score of a finite dataset degenerates into a nearest-neighbor lookup. While they address this by smoothing the score kernel, we show that autonomous flow models resolve it implicitly via a Riemannian preconditioner.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Equilibrium Dynamics &amp; Flow.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Du [33]</a></cite> introduced Equilibrium Matching (EqM) to replace time-dependent fields with a single time-invariant gradient. This parallels Action Matching <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>. Our analysis reveals that EqM is unique: it implements a natural gradient descent on the marginal energy. This connects EqM to the fundamental JKO scheme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, unifying “transport” and “restoration” under a single autonomous field.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Preliminaries: A Unified Schedule Formulation</h3>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To provide a general theory covering Diffusion Models (DDPM, EDM) and Flow Matching (EqM), we adopt the unified affine formulation proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. [30]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> index the noise level. The noisy observation <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is constructed from clean data <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and noise <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐈</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})</annotation></semantics></math> via method-specific schedule functions <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(t)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}_{t}=a(t)\mathbf{x}+b(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}_{t}=a(t)\mathbf{x}+b(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Assuming that the data is normalized, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at time <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is</p>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Generative models are typically trained to predict a linear target <math id="S3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t)=c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r(\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t)=c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE):</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(f)=\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}\left[\|f(\mathbf{u}_{t})-(c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|^{2}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐮</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(f)=\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon},t}\left[\|f(\mathbf{u}_{t})-(c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon})\|^{2}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the standard diffusion paradigm, <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is explicitly conditioned on the noise level <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e. it has the form<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          While a more accurate notation would have been <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math>, with some abuse of notation we use <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{t}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{t}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> to denote a function of <math id="footnote1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="footnote1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> to keep the notation consistent with the autonomous models.</span></span></span> <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{t}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{t}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>. The minimizer of the MSE loss is then the conditional expectation of the target:</p>
<table id="S3.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">This function defines a time-dependent vector field that guides the generation process.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, however, we focus on autonomous models where the network <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> receives only the noisy observation <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math>, with no access to <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. The minimizer of the MSE loss for such a “noise-agnostic” model is the <span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">posterior expectation</span> of the target (Lemma <a href="#Thmlemma1" title="Lemma 1 (Optimal Autonomous Target). ‣ A.1 Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S3.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]\right]=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}[f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})]." fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]\right]=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}[f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">This has a very intuitive interpretation: <span id="S3.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the optimal autonomous model is a time-average of the optimal conditional model with respect to the posterior <math id="S3.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u}).</annotation></semantics></math></span></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">By defining the optimal conditional denoiser as <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E[\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{u},t]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E[\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{u},t]</annotation></semantics></math>, we can expand this target as (Lemma <a href="#Thmlemma2" title="Lemma 2 (Denoiser Formulation). ‣ A.1 Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S3.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}+\left(c(t)-\frac{d(t)a(t)}{b(t)}\right)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}+\left(c(t)-\frac{d(t)a(t)}{b(t)}\right)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p5.2" class="ltx_p">Specific choices for the coefficients <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(t),b(t),c(t),d(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t),b(t),c(t),d(t)</annotation></semantics></math> yield standard architectures, as summarized in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3 Preliminaries: A Unified Schedule Formulation ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. In the table, DDPM formulation uses the so called variance preserving diffusion processes where coefficients <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(t)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfy <math id="S3.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{2}(t)+b^{2}(t)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{2}(t)+b^{2}(t)=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(t)=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(t)=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined via a discrete diffusion process that determine the form of <math id="S3.p5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\alpha}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\alpha}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">The central question of this paper is to understand the geometric and dynamical consequences of replacing the precise conditional field <math id="S3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> with this autonomous posterior average <math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>. Does this time-invariant field still define a valid generative trajectory?</em></p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In the following sections, we analyze its alignment with an energy landscape (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 The Geometry of the Marginal Energy ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) and deep dive into its properties when used as a generative model (Sections <a href="#S5" title="5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and <a href="#S6" title="6 Stability Conditions for Sampling with Autonomous Models ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>).</p>
</div>

<td id="S3.T1.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;">0</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;">1</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbf{u}-\sqrt{\overline{\alpha}_{t}}D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})}{\sqrt{1-\overline{\alpha}_{t}}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}[\epsilon_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><msqrt><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></msqrt><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msqrt></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>ϵ</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbf{u}-\sqrt{\overline{\alpha}_{t}}D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})}{\sqrt{1-\overline{\alpha}_{t}}}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}[\epsilon_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})]</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S3.T1.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">EDM</span></th>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;">1</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>σ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{t}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;">1</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;">0</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:6pt;padding-bottom:6pt;"><math id="S3.T1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T1.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
