</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>The Geometry of the Marginal Energy</h3>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Standard diffusion models rely on a time-dependent score function, <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)</annotation></semantics></math>, which explicitly guides the trajectory at every noise level. In contrast, <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">autonomous models</span> (such as Equilibrium Matching or “blind” diffusion) must compress these dynamics into a single, static vector field <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> that is independent of time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This fundamental difference raises a critical geometric question: <span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Does this static field align with the gradient of a global potential energy?</span> If such a potential exists, <span id="S4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">autonomous generation</span> could be theoretically grounded as a form of energy minimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The most natural candidate for this potential is the <span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">marginal energy</span> <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as the negative log-likelihood of the marginal data density <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mo>∫</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0em">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(\mathbf{u})=\int p(\mathbf{u}|t)p(t)dt</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log p(\mathbf{u})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=-\log p(\mathbf{u}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">To determine if the learned field <math id="S4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> aligns with this energy, we must first derive its gradient. By differentiating the marginal likelihood mixture, we find that the gradient of the marginal energy is the posterior expectation of the conditional scores:</p>
<table id="S4.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}[-\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}[-\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p3.3" class="ltx_p">We refer the reader to Lemma <a href="#Thmlemma3" title="Lemma 3 (Gradient of the Marginal Energy). ‣ A.2 Gradient of the Marginal Energy ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> for the proof. To evaluate this expectation, we use Tweedie’s formula <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> to express the conditional score in terms of the optimal denoiser:</p>
<table id="S4.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)=\frac{a(t)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})-\mathbf{u}}{b(t)^{2}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\log p(\mathbf{u}|t)=\frac{a(t)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})-\mathbf{u}}{b(t)^{2}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p3.4" class="ltx_p">Substituting this directly into the posterior expectation yields the explicit form of the marginal energy gradient:</p>
<table id="S4.E11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbf{u}-a(t)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})}{b(t)^{2}}\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbf{u}-a(t)D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})}{b(t)^{2}}\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p3.5" class="ltx_p">This result establishes the link between the static geometry and the dynamic denoising process. However, it also exposes a critical flaw in the landscape itself.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>The Energy Paradox</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key requirement for generative modeling is that the learned vector field <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> must be consistent with the clean data support. Depending on the specific formulation, the field at the boundary (<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>) generally behaves in one of two ways:</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Case 1: Attractors (EqM, EDM).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For equilibrium-based models, the target is the data itself or a restoration term. Here, the ideal field must vanish at the clean data (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>𝟎</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{0}</annotation></semantics></math>) to create a stable fixed point.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Case 2: Transversal Flows (Flow Matching).</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For transport-based models, the target is a velocity vector (e.g., <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>). At the data, the field does not vanish but converges to a finite, non-zero velocity vector (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\approx\mathbf{0}-\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mn>𝟎</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{x})\approx\mathbf{0}-\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>) that ensures the trajectory intersects the data manifold at the correct time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The Singularity.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Regardless of whether the field acts as an attractor or a transversal flow, the model faces a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">geometric singularity</span>. As established in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Concentration of 𝑝(𝑡|𝐮) via Proximity ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, the posterior <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> collapses near the data manifold. The term inside the expectation in Equation (<a href="#S4.E11" title="In 4 The Geometry of the Marginal Energy ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>) has a singularity as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, the marginal energy forms an infinitely deep potential well (<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}\to-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}\to-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, see Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ The Singularity. ‣ 4.1 The Energy Paradox ‣ 4 The Geometry of the Marginal Energy ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), causing the associated gradient field to diverge:</p>
<table id="S4.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim_{\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{x}_{k}}\|\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\|=\infty." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">lim</mo><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mrow><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></msub><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim_{\mathbf{u}\to\mathbf{x}_{k}}\|\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\|=\infty.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This creates a puzzle: how can a neural network learn a bounded vector field (which must be finite at the data) that aligns with a geometry defined by such a singular potential?</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One might argue that in practice, training is stabilized by truncating the noise level at some <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t_{min}&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t_{min}&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> (the “ill-conditioned regime”). However, this does not resolve the geometric paradox; it merely converts a mathematical singularity into an extremely stiff optimization landscape where Hessian eigenvalues scale as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1/t_{min}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><msubsup><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1/t_{min}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. Whether strictly singular or merely ill-conditioned, the raw energy landscape essentially forbids stable gradient descent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the next section, we resolve this puzzle by showing that noise-blind models do not follow the raw energy gradient, but rather a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Riemannian gradient flow</span> that perfectly preconditions this singularity.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18428v1/marginal_energy.svg" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/191;" width="405" height="191"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S4.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Singular Geometry of the Marginal Energy Landscape.</span> (Left) 3D Energy Landscape: A visualization of the marginal energy <math id="S4.F1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{marg}(u)=-\log p(u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">−</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{marg}(u)=-\log p(u)</annotation></semantics></math>. The landscape reveals an infinitely deep potential well at the data manifold, where the energy diverges to <math id="S4.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.
(Right) Contour View: Top-down perspective showing the energy concentration around discrete data points (stars). While the raw gradient <math id="S4.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{u}E_{marg}(u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>u</mi></msub><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{u}E_{marg}(u)</annotation></semantics></math> becomes singular as <math id="S4.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="u" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>u</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">u</annotation></semantics></math> approaches the clean data, in this work we prove that autonomous models remain stable by implicitly implementing a Riemannian gradient flow. In this framework, the posterior noise variance acts as a local conformal metric that preconditions and perfectly counteracts the geometric singularity.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow</h3>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We resolve the paradox of stable convergence despite divergent gradients by showing that autonomous models implement a Riemannian gradient flow. We show that the learned vector field <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> is structurally identical to the natural gradient of the marginal energy, but with a critical correction term that dominates only when geometric concentration fails.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>The Anatomy of the Autonomous Field</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recall from Lemma <a href="#Thmlemma2" title="Lemma 2 (Denoiser Formulation). ‣ A.1 Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target ‣ Appendix A General Derivations for Autonomous Models ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> that the optimal autonomous field is given by:</p>
<table id="S5.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}+\frac{c(t)b(t)-d(t)a(t)}{b(t)}D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>D</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbb{E}_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}+\frac{c(t)b(t)-d(t)a(t)}{b(t)}D_{t}^{*}(\mathbf{u})\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This formulation reveals that for any affine schedule, the autonomous vector field is driven by two competing forces:</p>
<ol id="S5.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S5.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Repulsive Expansion</span> (<math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d(t)}{b(t)}\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math>): A linear term scaling with the noise geometry. Assuming standard diffusion signs (<math id="S5.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d,b&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d,b&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>), this pushes trajectories outward, accounting for the expanding volume of the noise distribution.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The Relative Restoration</span>: A denoising term pulling the sample towards high-density data regions. Its magnitude is modulated by the signal-to-noise ratio (defined in Equation (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3 Preliminaries: A Unified Schedule Formulation ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)) and the specific target coefficients <math id="S5.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c(t),d(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c(t),d(t)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The Energy-Aligned Decomposition.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand how these forces align with the geometry of the marginal energy <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we apply the properties of covariance to Eq. (<a href="#S5.E13" title="In 5.1 The Anatomy of the Autonomous Field ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>). As derived in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Derivation of General Energy-Aligned Decomposition ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>, the vector field decomposes into exactly three geometric components:</p>
<table id="S5.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\underbrace{\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})}_{\text{Natural Gradient}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]}_{\text{Transport Correction}}+\underbrace{\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}}_{\text{Linear Drift}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>E</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Natural Gradient</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" Correction</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" Drift</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\underbrace{\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})}_{\text{Natural Gradient}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]}_{\text{Transport Correction}}+\underbrace{\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}}_{\text{Linear Drift}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t|u}[c(t)/a(t)]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t|u}[c(t)/a(t)]</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean drift, <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">effective gradient gain</span> and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> is its time average defined as:</p>
<table id="S5.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda(t)\triangleq\frac{b(t)}{a(t)}\left(d(t)a(t)-c(t)b(t)\right),\quad\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t|u}[\lambda(t)]." display="block" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo
