encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda(t)\triangleq\frac{b(t)}{a(t)}\left(d(t)a(t)-c(t)b(t)\right),\quad\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{t|u}[\lambda(t)].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">This decomposition (Eq.<a href="#S5.E14" title="In The Energy-Aligned Decomposition. ‣ 5.1 The Anatomy of the Autonomous Field ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>) resolves the paradox by isolating the model’s behavior into interpretable geometric terms. The field is a Riemannian flow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite> (via the gain <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>) modified by a Transport Correction (covariance) term.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Importantly, this formulation exposes the mechanism of stability. While both the marginal energy gradient <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math> and the conditional energy gradient <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> become singular near the manifold (diverging as <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math>), as shown in detail in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Analysis of Specific Architectures: Exact Low-Noise Asymptotics ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, the effective gain <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda(t)</annotation></semantics></math> acts as a <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">perfect preconditioner</span>. It vanishes at a rate that exactly counteracts the divergence of the gradients, ensuring the product remains bounded.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In what follows, we show that the correction term vanishes in two key asymptotic regimes: <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">global high-dimensional concentration</span> (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Regime I: Global Concentration in High Dimensions ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>) and <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">local near-manifold proximity</span> (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS3" title="5.3 Regime II: Local Stability via Proximity ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.3</span></a>). In both limits, the posterior <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> concentrates, simplifying the dynamics to a pure, preconditioned natural gradient flow.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Regime I: Global Concentration in High Dimensions</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A central mystery of autonomous models is how a single vector field can “know” which noise level to apply to a given input without explicit conditioning. We resolve this by observing that in high-dimensional spaces (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\gg 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\gg 1</annotation></semantics></math>), provided the data resides on a low-dimensional manifold (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\ll D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\ll D</annotation></semantics></math>), the noise level <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> is not truly hidden; it is globally encoded in the geometry of the observation <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In these high-dimensional settings, the mass of a Gaussian distribution concentrates in a thin spherical shell <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>. When the data is low-dimensional, the noisy observation <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> can be decomposed into a component within the data subspace and an orthogonal noise component. Because the codimension is large, the magnitude of this orthogonal noise dominates the total norm. In this regime, the “shells” corresponding to different noise levels <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b(t)</annotation></semantics></math> become effectively disjoint. For completeness we provide a proof of this in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Posterior Concentration in High Dimensions ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As a result, the input <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> becomes a deterministic proxy for the noise level <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. This geometric structure has two profound consequences for the model’s objective:</p>
<ul id="S5.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Posterior Concentration:</span> The model’s uncertainty about the noise level vanishes. The posterior <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> collapses to a Dirac delta centered at an implicit estimate <math id="S5.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{t}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{t}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Vanishing Transport Correction:</span> Because there is no longer a mixture of conflicting noise levels at any given point, the complex interaction between different potential fields disappears. The transport correction term vanishes:</p>
<table id="S5.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]\to\mathbf{0}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>𝟎</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]\to\mathbf{0}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Consequently, in high dimensions, the field is strictly dominated by the <span id="S5.SS2.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Natural Gradient</span> flow:</p>
<table id="S5.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E17.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})\approx\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})+\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})\approx\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})+\overline{c}_{scale}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.3" class="ltx_p">This resolves the “blindness” paradox globally: the model implicitly sees <math id="S5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> through the separation of noise scales.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Regime II: Local Stability via Proximity</h4>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While high-dimensional concentration provides a global mechanism, a second, stronger mechanism ensures stability as the trajectory approaches the data, <em id="S5.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regardless of dimension</em>. We analyze the decomposition in the near-manifold limit:</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">1. The Near-Manifold Regime (Concentration via Proximity)</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As the observation <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐮</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}</annotation></semantics></math> approaches the data support (<math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{u}\to\mathcal{X}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{u}\to\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>), the likelihood becomes dominated by the smallest noise scales. This causes the posterior <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> to concentrate sharply on <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\rightarrow 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\rightarrow 0</annotation></semantics></math> simply because the observation is indistinguishable from clean data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We rigorously prove this in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Concentration of 𝑝(𝑡|𝐮) via Proximity ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> for two cases. In the first case, we assume that the data is discrete and finite. In this case, we show that as we approach a data point, the posterior <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> converges weakly to the Dirac measure <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta(t)</annotation></semantics></math>. In the second case, we assume that the data lies on a manifold of dimension <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> in an ambient space of dimension <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D-d&gt;2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D-d&gt;2</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that we do not require <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\gg d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>≫</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\gg d</annotation></semantics></math> as in Section <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Regime I: Global Concentration in High Dimensions ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>. In this case as in the case for discrete data, we can show the weak convergence of <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> as we approach the data manifold.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, this <span id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">local concentration</span> occurs even in low dimensions. Therefore, as we approach the data manifold, the transport correction term in the autonomous field becomes negligible:</p>
<table id="S5.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]\to\mathbf{0}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>𝟎</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{t|u}\left[\left(\lambda(t)-\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})\right)\left(\nabla E_{t}(\mathbf{u})-\nabla E_{\text{marg}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\right]\to\mathbf{0}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">In this limit, the raw energy gradients (<math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>) diverge at an <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math> rate, creating a potential geometric singularity. However, the field remains stable because the effective gain implements a Riemannian preconditioning:</p>
<ul id="S5.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Geometric Preconditioning:</span> The effective gain <math id="S5.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="true">¯</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\overline{\lambda}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> vanishes at a rate that exactly matches the divergence of the gradients (<math id="S5.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{\text{marg}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mtext>marg</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{\text{marg}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.I3.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla E_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla E_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>), neutralizing the infinity.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S5.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.I3.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Singularity Absorption:</span> In transport-based models (e.g., Flow Matching), the linear drift term acts as a counter-force that effectively “absorbs” any residual singular component of the energy gradient, resulting in a smooth, finite velocity.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">2. The High-Noise Regime (Transport Dominated)</h5>

<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Far from the data manifold, if the dimension <math id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math> is not sufficiently large to enforce global concentration (Sec. <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Regime I: Global Concentration in High Dimensions ‣ 5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>), the strict proximity cue is absent. Here, the covariance term becomes significant, “steering” the trajectories away from the raw energy gradient. This rotation ensures the field satisfies the global transport requirements of the noise schedule before the local geometry takes over.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the exact low-noise asymptotic derivations and verification that architectures like Equilibrium Matching and Flow Matching satisfy these bounded field conditions, see Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Analysis of Specific Architectures: Exact Low-Noise Asymptotics ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While we showed that the target field is bounded and very close to the optimal conditional field in certain regimes, the dynamics used to generate samples are sensitive to the integrator’s step size and coefficients. A bounded target divided by a vanishing noise scale creates a stiff differential equation resulting in instabilities. We discuss this in the next section.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Stability Conditions for Sampling with Autonomous Models</h3>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> established that the optimal autonomous target <math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> is geometrically well-behaved and acts as an accurate proxy for the conditional field in regimes of concentration (high dimensions or near-manifold), this does not guarantee stable generation. The <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">dynamics</span> of the sampling process can amplify small errors into divergent trajectories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To quantify this, we analyze the sampling process as the integration of a time-dependent velocity field <math id="S6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐯</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S6.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{dt}=\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)\triangleq\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}(\mathbf{u})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{d\mathbf{u}}{dt}=\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)\triangleq\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}(\mathbf{u}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="S6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the drift coefficient of the noise schedule and <math id="S6.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> is the <span id="S6.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">effective gain</span> of the parameterization (derived in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Derivation of Stability Conditions ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>). Note that even though the autonomous model <math id="S6.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> is time-independent, the sampler velocity <math id="S6.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math> remains a function of time because the schedule coefficients <math id="S6.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> vary during integration.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We compare this autonomous velocity against an ideal “Oracle” sampler that has access to the exact noise level <math id="S6.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. The structural stability is determined by the <span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Drift Perturbation Error</span> <math id="S6.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math>, which measures the deviation caused by substituting the conditional target with the autonomous approximation:</p>
<table id="S6.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S6.E20"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S6.E20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{orc}(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{orc}(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S6.E20.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S6.E21"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S6.E21.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S6.E21.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mu(t)\mathbf{u}+\nu(t)f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Subtracting the two eliminates the linear term, isolating the error introduced by the target parameterization:</p>
<table id="S6.E22" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S6.E22.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{u},t)\triangleq\|\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)-\mathbf{v}_{orc}(\mathbf{u},t)\|=\underbrace{|\nu(t)|}_{\text{Gain}}\cdot\underbrace{\|f^{*}(\mathbf{u})-f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})\|}_{\text{Estimation Error}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≜</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐯</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Gain</mtext></munder><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>f</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Estimation Error</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{u},t)\triangleq\|\mathbf{v}_{aut}(\mathbf{u},t)-\mathbf{v}_{orc}(\mathbf{u},t)\|=\underbrace{|\nu(t)|}_{\text{Gain}}\cdot\underbrace{\|f^{*}(\mathbf{u})-f^{*}_{t}(\mathbf{u})\|}_{\text{Estimation Error}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S6.p3.3" class="ltx_p">This decomposition reveals that stability is a race condition as <math id="S6.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>: the estimation error (posterior uncertainty) naturally tends to zero, but the effective gain <math id="S6.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> may diverge. We analyze this competition for three standard parameterizations. Detailed derivations can be found in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Derivation of Stability Conditions ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>:</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S6.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Noise Prediction (DDPM/DDIM):</span> The effective gain scales inversely with the noise standard deviation (<math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)\propto 1/b(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)\propto 1/b(t)</annotation></semantics></math>). As <math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>, this singularity amplifies the finite <span id="S6.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“Jensen Gap”</span> as defined in Equation (<a href="#A6.E66" title="In Case 1: Noise Prediction (DDPM/DDIM) ‣ F.2 Stability Analysis by Parameterization ‣ Appendix F Derivation of Stability Conditions ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">66</span></a>)—the mismatch between the harmonic mean of noise levels and the true noise level—causing the error to diverge (<math id="S6.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim\Delta\mathbf{v}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim\Delta\mathbf{v}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Signal Prediction (EDM):</span> The gain contains a stronger singularity (<math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)\propto 1/b(t)^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∝</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)\propto 1/b(t)^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>). However, the error in the signal estimator vanishes <span id="S6.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">exponentially</span> fast near the discrete data manifold. This rapid convergence counteracts the polynomial divergence of the gain, resulting in a stable flow (<math id="S6.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lim\Delta\mathbf{v}\to 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">lim</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lim\Delta\mathbf{v}\to 0</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Velocity Prediction (Flow Matching):</span> The update is identity-mapped with a bounded gain (<math id="S6.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)=1</annotation></semantics></math>). There are no singular coefficients to amplify errors. The dynamics absorb posterior uncertainty into a bounded effective drift, making this parameterization inherently stable.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S6.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 6 Stability Conditions for Sampling with Autonomous Models ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes these regimes. It is important to note that this analysis identifies <span id="S6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sufficient conditions for instability</span>. A divergence (<math id="S6.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{v}\to\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐯</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{v}\to\infty</annotation></semantics></math>) guarantees failure, whereas a bounded error is a necessary (but not strictly sufficient) condition for high-fidelity generation. Our results prove that velocity-based parameterizations satisfy this necessary condition, whereas noise prediction structurally fails for autonomous models.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Summary of Stability Analysis for Autonomous Models. The Drift Perturbation Error is the product of the Effective Gain <math id="S6.T2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)</annotation></semantics></math> and the estimation error. Detailed derivations are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Derivation of Stability Conditions ‣ Appendices ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</figcaption>
<table id="S6.T2.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S6.T2.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parameterization</span></th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effective Gain</span> <math id="S6.T2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error Mechanism</span></th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stability</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S6.T2.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Noise (<math id="S6.T2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}</annotation></semantics></math>)</th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><math id="S6.T2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="S6.T2.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Amplified Jensen Gap</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;">Unstable</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T2.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Signal (<math id="S6.T2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math>)</th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><math id="S6.T2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t)^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t)^{2})</annotation></semantics></math></th>
<td id="S6.T2.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Exp. Decay vs. Poly. Div.</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;">Stable</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S6.T2.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S6.T2.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_b" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Velocity (<math id="S6.T2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{v}</annotation></semantics></math>)</th>
<th id="S6.T2.2.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_row ltx_border_b" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><math id="S6.T2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>𝟏</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{1}</annotation></semantics></math> (Bounded)</th>
<td id="S6.T2.2.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;">Bounded Drift</td>
<td id="S6.T2.2.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding-top:2.5pt;padding-bottom:2.5pt;"><span id="S6.T2.2.4.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#009900;">Inherently Stable</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Empirical Verification</h3>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To validate the theoretical stability conditions derived in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Stability Conditions for Sampling with Autonomous Models ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we conducted experiments on CIFAR-10, SVHN and Fashion MNIST datasets. The primary objective was to determine if the predicted structural instability of autonomous noise-prediction models (DDPM Blind) manifests in standard image benchmarks, and whether velocity-based parameterizations (Flow Matching) can resolve this paradox without explicit noise conditioning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h4>

<div id="S7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We trained four model configurations using a ResNet-based U-Net architecture. All models were trained for 10,000 steps using EMA=0.999 and batch size=128.</p>
<ul id="S7.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S7.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DDPM Blind (Autonomous):</span> A noise-prediction model where time-level conditioning is removed.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DDPM Conditional:</span> The standard baseline utilizing explicit time embeddings.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flow Matching Blind (Autonomous):</span> A velocity-parameterized model (<math id="S7.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v=\dot{u}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>u</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v=\dot{u}</annotation></semantics></math>) without noise-level conditioning.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Flow Matching Conditional:</span> A velocity-based model with explicit <math id="S7.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> conditioning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Findings: Parameterization and Stability.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The generative results align with our theoretical stability analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S7.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S7.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unstable Noise Prediction:</span> As predicted in Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Stability Conditions for Sampling with Autonomous Models ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, the <span id="S7.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">DDPM Blind</span> model fails to generate coherent samples. The resulting images are dominated by high-frequency artifacts and residual noise, confirming that the <math id="S7.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math> gain singularity in noise-prediction acts as an amplifier for estimation errors.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S7.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stable Velocity Flows:</span> In contrast, the <span id="S7.I2.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Flow Matching Blind</span> model produces sharp samples qualitatively similar to its conditional counterpart. Because the gain remains bounded (<math id="S7.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nu(t)=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>ν</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nu(t)=1</annotation></semantics></math>), the dynamics absorb posterior uncertainty into a stable effective drift.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">These findings demonstrate that while the marginal energy landscape contains a fundamental singularity, velocity-based architectures remain stable by implicitly implementing a Riemannian gradient flow that preconditions the landscape.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</section>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.2 </span>The Impact of Dimensionality on Autonomous Generation</h4>

<div id="S7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To empirically illustrate how high-dimensional geometry resolves the ambiguity of autonomous generation, we designed a controlled toy experiment motivated by the setup in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. We constructed a 2D concentric circles dataset and embedded it into a high-dimensional ambient space <math id="S7.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{D}</annotation></semantics></math> using a random orthogonal projection matrix <math id="S7.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times 2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times 2}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S7.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P^{T}P=I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>I</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P^{T}P=I</annotation></semantics></math>. We trained a standard residual network for both Flow Matching and DDPM under conditional and autonomous (“blind”) settings. For the conditional variants, the network received the true time embedding <math id="S7.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas for the autonomous variants, <math id="S7.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> was strictly zeroed out, forcing the network to implicitly infer the noise scale from the spatial coordinates alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S7.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 7.2 The Impact of Dimensionality on Autonomous Generation ‣ 7 Empirical Verification ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> visualizes the generated samples projected back down to the 2D subspace across exponentially increasing ambient dimensions (<math id="S7.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\in\{2,8,32,128\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\in\{2,8,32,128\}</annotation></semantics></math>). The results highlight three distinct geometric regimes that perfectly mirror our theoretical stability analysis:</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S7.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S7.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The low-dimensional ambiguity regime (<math id="S7.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=2</annotation></semantics></math>). In low dimensions, both <span id="S7.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">autonomous models</span> struggle to capture the true distribution. Because the noise shells heavily overlap, the posterior noise distribution <math id="S7.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|u)</annotation></semantics></math> is highly ambiguous, resulting in diffuse, noisy sampling. The network lacks the geometric cues necessary to separate noise scales.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The parameterization stability regime (<math id="S7.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D\in\{8,32\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D\in\{8,32\}</annotation></semantics></math>). As the ambient dimension increases, probability mass begins to concentrate into disjoint shells, giving the network implicit cues about the noise scale. In these moderate dimensions, both models successfully begin to resolve the global ring structure. However, the structural stability of the underlying parameterization dictates the precision of the generated samples. Autonomous Flow Matching (FM Blind) leverages its bounded velocity target to smoothly absorb residual posterior uncertainty, resulting in tight, clean concentric circles as early as <math id="S7.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=8" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=8</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, DDPM Blind exhibits noticeably higher variance and background scatter. This empirically demonstrates that the <math id="S7.I3.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math> gain in noise-prediction architectures acts as an amplifier for residual estimation errors, leading to noisier sampling trajectories before absolute concentration is reached.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S7.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S7.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The absolute concentration regime (<math id="S7.I3.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=128</annotation></semantics></math>). In extreme high dimensions, the geometric concentration becomes so sharp that the posterior <math id="S7.I3.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|u)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|u)</annotation></semantics></math> effectively collapses to a Dirac delta. Consequently, the network’s estimation error of the noise scale vanishes. Because the estimation error drops to zero faster than the DDPM gain diverges, even the structurally unstable DDPM Blind model eventually produces clean, coherent samples.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S7.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18428v1/toy_circes-L_t-norm-v3_Ddim-2.svg" id="S7.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/80;" width="452" height="80"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18428v1/toy_circes-L_t-norm-v3_Ddim-8.svg" id="S7.F5.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/80;" width="452" height="80"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18428v1/toy_circes-L_t-norm-v3_Ddim-32.svg" id="S7.F5.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/80;" width="452" height="80"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18428v1/toy_circes-L_t-norm-v3_Ddim-128.svg" id="S7.F5.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/80;" width="452" height="80"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S7.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generative performance on a 2D concentric circles dataset embedded in <math id="S7.F5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{D}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span> Conditional models receive explicit time embeddings, while autonomous (blind) models must implicitly infer the noise scale. At low dimensions (<math id="S7.F5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=2</annotation></semantics></math>, top), blind models fail due to overlapping noise distributions. At moderate dimensions (<math id="S7.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=8,32" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=8,32</annotation></semantics></math>, middle), Flow Matching achieves stable generation due to its bounded velocity parameterization, while DDPM Blind exhibits severe noise artifacts due to its singular gain <math id="S7.F5.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(1/b(t))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(1/b(t))</annotation></semantics></math>. At extreme dimensions (<math id="S7.F5.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D=128" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D=128</annotation></semantics></math>, bottom), absolute geometric concentration forces the estimation error to zero, allowing both blind models to converge.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S7.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">7.3 </span>Experiments with more realistic datasets</h4>

<div id="S7.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We verify our stability analysis against the benchmark results of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. [30]</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Quantitative Results.</h5>

<div id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S7.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Quantitative Results. ‣ 7.3 Experiments with more realistic datasets ‣ 7 Empirical Verification ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> confirms the theory on CIFAR-10. The failure of DDIM (FID 40.90) is not due to a lack of expressivity, but due to the structural instability of the parameterization. Velocity-based models (EqM, uEDM) achieve state-of-the-art performance by ensuring the learned field implicitly incorporates the Riemannian metric discussed in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Autonomous Generation as Riemannian Gradient Flow ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S7.T3" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>Conclusion</h3>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have identified the marginal energy as the implicit objective of autonomous generative models and proved that its landscape contains a fundamental gradient singularity at the data manifold. We demonstrated that these models effectively implement a Riemannian gradient flow, where the posterior noise variance acts as a local conformal metric that preconditions the singular energy. Finally, we derived the bounded vector field condition, proving that velocity-based parameterizations are mathematically necessary to realize this stable flow in the absence of explicit noise conditioning. By shifting the generative task from time-dependent score matching to time-invariant energy alignment, our work provides a rigorous geometric foundation for the next generation of autonomous and equilibrium-based models.</p>
</div>
</section>

<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>General Derivations for Autonomous Models</h3>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Derivation of the Optimal Autonomous Target</h4>

<div id="Thmlemma1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_lemma">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmlemma1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lemma 1</span></span><span id="Thmlemma1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold"> </span>(Optimal Autonomous Target)<span id="Thmlemma1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmlemma1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmlemma1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmlemma1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Consider the loss functional <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(f)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(f)</annotation></semantics></math> defined in Eq (<a href="#S3.E4" title="In 3 Preliminaries: A Unified Schedule Formulation ‣ The Geometry of Noise: Why Diffusion Models Don’t Need Noise Conditioning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). The unique global minimizer <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math> is given by the expectation of the target conditioned on the noise level <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, weighted by the posterior <math id="Thmlemma1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(t|\mathbf{u})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(t|\mathbf{u})</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="A1.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]\right]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐮</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.1389em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0.1389em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">𝔼</mo><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mo fence="false">|</mo><mi>𝐮</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐱</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f^{*}(\mathbf{u})=\E_{t|\mathbf{u}}\left[\E_{\mathbf{x},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}|\mathbf{u},t}[c(t)\mathbf{x}+d(t)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}]\right].</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<div id="A1.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">This is an application of the Law of Iterated Expectations.
∎</span></p>
